STUB
# Exporting

Frame Job writes the timeline out as a movie, an audio file or an animated image, and saves single frames as stills. One export sheet covers every format. You choose the format, then the size, frame rate, quality, loudness and range, and the sheet shows what the file will be before anything is written. Exports can run at once behind a progress sheet, or wait in the Export Queue while you keep editing. Every export of a file with sound reports what that sound measured.

## Opening the export sheet

Choose **File ▸ Export…** (⌘E), or click **Export…** at the right end of the toolbar. Playback pauses and the sheet opens over the editor window.

The command is greyed out while the timeline is empty. An export always writes the whole top-level timeline, even when you are working inside a nest.

The sheet reopens on the **last choices you exported with**. Clicking **Export…** or **Add to Queue** records them; Cancel does not. With nothing remembered, it opens on H.264 at the document's own size.

The remembered choice belongs to the app, not to the project, so every document's sheet opens on it. A remembered **In/out range** falls back to **Whole project** on a document that has no range.

## The controls

From top to bottom:

| Control | What it does | Default |
|---|---|---|
| **Preset** | Applies a saved set of choices (see [Presets](#presets)). The gear beside it saves and deletes presets. | Custom |
| **Format** | The encoding: container and codec together. | H.264 (MP4) |
| **Dynamic Range** | Shown only in an HDR (HLG) project. See [HDR projects](#hdr-projects). | HDR (HLG) |
| **Speed** | How long the AV1 encoder works on each frame. See [Speed](#speed). | Balanced |
| **Size** | The frame size, or **Custom…** with width and height fields on the row below. | The format's first row |
| **Frame rate** | **Project rate**, or a fixed rate. | Project rate |
| **Quality** | **Format default**, or a bit-rate tier. | Format default |
| **Bit depth** | **16-bit** or **24-bit**, for WAV and AIFF. See [Bit depth](#bit-depth). | 16-bit |
| **Stems** | **None**, **One per Track** or **One per Track Name**: also write each track's sound as its own file, for the audio formats. See [Stems](#stems). | None |
| **Loudness** | **Off**, a loudness target, or **Custom…** with a LUFS field. | Off |
| **Range** | **Whole project**, or **In/out range** when one is set. | Whole project |
| **Burn in timecode** | Draws the project timecode into the picture. | Off |

Under the controls, a readout line describes the file and a footnote names the codec, the container and the rates the file will use. Every number they show is the size, rate and duration the file will actually have.

- **Readout:** `1920 × 1080 · 30 fps · 00:01:12:05` (size, frame rate, duration). For the audio-only formats it reads `Audio only · 00:01:12.200`. For GIF and APNG it adds the frame count: `· 360 frames, no audio`. For **AV1 (MP4)**, **AV1 (WebM)**, **VP9 (WebM)** and **VP9 with Alpha (WebM)** a second line estimates how long the export will take: `Estimated time: about 25 s` (in 5-second steps under a minute, then minutes, then hours and minutes). It follows the format, Speed, size and range, and it is only an estimate: the figures behind it are the median of three measured exports per format at 1080p and 4K, of real 4K camera footage on an idle Apple M2 Max, so a slower or busy Mac, or a heavy timeline, takes longer. The other formats show no estimate.
- **Footnote:** the codec, the container (left out when it is the same word, as in `GIF`), the AV1 speed (`AV1 · MP4 · Balanced`, `AV1 · WEBM · Balanced`; VP9 has none: `VP9 · WEBM`, `VP9 · WEBM · alpha`), the video rate, the audio rate (`192 kbps audio`), `24-bit` for a 24-bit WAV or AIFF, the loudness target (`−14 LUFS`) and `alpha` when the format keeps transparency. When you pick a Quality tier and the format sets its own rate, it reads `format's own rate` instead of a number.

A control the chosen format cannot use is greyed out rather than hidden. Its value is not sent.

### Format

| Format | Container | What it is for |
|---|---|---|
| H.264 (MP4) | `.mp4` | The everyday delivery file. 8-bit. |
| HEVC (MP4) | `.mp4` | A smaller file at the same picture. 8-bit (Main profile). |
| HEVC with Alpha (MOV) | `.mov` | A small delivery file that keeps a transparent canvas, for laying over another background. 8-bit. |
| HEVC 10-bit (MP4) | `.mp4` | Keeps a 10-bit source's gradients (Main 10). |
| AV1 (MP4) | `.mp4` | The smallest delivery file, encoded by the AV1 encoder built into Frame Job. 10-bit, and it can carry HDR. Slower to export than HEVC. See [Speed](#speed). |
| AV1 (WebM) | `.webm` | The same AV1 picture in a WebM file, with Opus sound, for the web. Frame Job writes the WebM itself. |
| VP9 (WebM) | `.webm` | VP9 in a WebM file, with Opus sound: the web format every browser plays, encoded by the VP9 encoder built into Frame Job. 8-bit, or 10-bit when it carries HDR. Slower to export than HEVC and larger than AV1 for the same picture. |
| VP9 with Alpha (WebM) | `.webm` | VP9 (WebM) that keeps a transparent canvas, for a title or a lower third a web page plays over its own background in Chrome or Firefox. 8-bit, always the SDR picture. Safari's transparent movie is HEVC with Alpha. |
| ProRes 422 (MOV) | `.mov` | An editing master for another application. 10-bit. |
| ProRes 4444 (MOV) | `.mov` | A master that keeps the alpha channel. 12-bit. |
| Audio only (M4A) | `.m4a` | AAC sound only. |
| Audio only (WAV) | `.wav` | Uncompressed 16-bit or 24-bit, 48 kHz sound. |
| Audio only (AIFF) | `.aiff` | The same samples as WAV, in an AIFF file. |
| Animated GIF | `.gif` | A short silent loop. Capped at 480 × 270 and 12.5 fps by default. |
| Animated PNG | `.png` | A lossless silent loop with real transparency. Capped at 960 × 540 and 25 fps by default. |

Sound in the movie formats is stereo at 48 kHz: AAC in H.264, HEVC, HEVC with Alpha and AV1 (MP4), Opus in AV1 (WebM) and both VP9 formats, and 16-bit LPCM in both ProRes formats. A project with no sound exports a WebM with no sound track. GIF and APNG carry no sound. A file's sound is exactly as long as the range it exports, including when a clip in it plays faster or slower.

Changing the format rebuilds the Size list and puts it back on that format's default. Your frame rate, quality, loudness and range choices stay as they were.

### Size

The Size popup lists, in order:

- **GIF default** or **APNG default**: the format's cap. Only on those two formats, and it is their default.
- **Document size**: the canvas as it is. On a format that needs even dimensions and a canvas with an odd edge, this row is named **Document (even)** and is one pixel smaller on that edge.
- **4K**, **1440p**, **1080p**, **720p**: the number is the short edge. The long edge follows the document's shape, rounded to an even number, so a vertical project's 1080p is 1080 × 1920.
- **Custom…**: type a width and a height, each from 16 to 8192 pixels. The fields start from the size that was chosen a moment before.

A row with the same numbers as an earlier row is hidden, so a 1920 × 1080 document shows Document size and no separate 1080p. Sizes larger than the document are offered, so a 720p recording can be exported at 4K.

How the picture fits the frame:

- **Even dimensions.** H.264, HEVC, HEVC with Alpha, HEVC 10-bit, both AV1 formats, both VP9 formats and ProRes 422 need them, so an odd width or height is written one pixel smaller. ProRes 4444, GIF and APNG keep an odd edge.
- **Movies** are written at exactly the size you choose. When that size is within a pixel of the canvas's shape, the picture fills the frame edge to edge. Any other shape is letterboxed with black.
- **ProRes 4444, HEVC with Alpha and VP9 with Alpha (WebM)** refuse a size of a different shape instead of letterboxing it, because the padding would destroy the alpha channel. Every row in the Size popup has the canvas's shape, so this only happens with a Custom size.
- **GIF and APNG** fit the picture inside the size you choose, keeping its shape and never enlarging it. The readout shows the size the file will have: a 1080 × 1920 project's GIF default is 152 × 270.

The Size control is greyed out for the audio-only formats.

### Speed

The **Speed** row sits under Format (under Dynamic Range in an HDR project). It is live only on **AV1 (MP4)** and **AV1 (WebM)**; on every other format it is greyed out and keeps your last choice. **VP9 (WebM)** and **VP9 with Alpha (WebM)** have one speed, so the row is greyed out there too.

| Choice | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Faster** | The quickest AV1 export and the largest file. On 10 seconds of 4K camera footage it took about half Balanced's time (7.1 s against 14.0 s on an Apple M2 Max) and wrote a file 27 % larger; at 1080p 2.4 s against 4.2 s, 4 % larger. |
| **Balanced** | The default. |
| **Smaller file** | The slowest AV1 export and the smallest file. On the same footage it took about 1.4 times Balanced's time (19.9 s against 14.0 s at 4K, 5.8 s against 4.2 s at 1080p) and wrote a file 12 % smaller at 4K, 5 % smaller at 1080p. |

AV1 and VP9 are encoded in software, so they take longer than the HEVC formats, which use the Mac's hardware encoder. The choice is remembered with the rest of the sheet and stored in presets.

### Frame rate

**Project rate** exports at the document's frame rate, or at the format's own rate for GIF (12.5 fps) and APNG (25 fps). The fixed choices are 24, 23.976, 25, 30, 29.97, 50 and 60 fps. Greyed out for the audio-only formats.

### Quality

**Format default** lets the encoder choose the video rate. The sound uses 192 kbps AAC, or 192 kbps Opus in the two WebM formats.

The four tiers set a video rate from the frame's size, so a tier means the same picture quality at every size. Each tier's title shows the rate it would ask for at the size and frame rate now chosen.

| Tier | Video at 1080p, 30 fps or less (H.264) | AAC sound |
|---|---|---|
| **Low** | 4.0 Mbps | 128 kbps |
| **Medium** | 6.0 Mbps | 192 kbps |
| **High** | 8.0 Mbps | 256 kbps |
| **Maximum** | 12.0 Mbps | 320 kbps |

- The video rate scales with the frame's area. High is about 3.6 Mbps at 720p and 32 Mbps at 4K.
- Above 30 fps, the video rate is 1.5 times higher.
- HEVC formats, AV1 and VP9 ask for 60 % of the H.264 rate. AV1's and VP9's **Format default** is the HEVC rate too.
- For **AV1** the rate is a soft cap. AV1 encodes at a constant quality chosen to match or beat HEVC at that rate, so it usually stays under the rate and simple footage comes out much smaller. Very detailed footage can go over: up to about 1.25 times the rate was measured. Its tier titles and footnote read `usually ≤ …`.
- For **VP9 (WebM)** the rate is a soft cap the same way: VP9 encodes at a constant quality chosen to match or beat HEVC at that rate (HEVC 10-bit's in an HDR export), and the file usually stays under it. Up to about 1.15 times the rate was measured. Its tier titles and footnote read `usually ≤ …` too. On **VP9 with Alpha (WebM)** the rate is the picture's alone: the transparency is a second stream at a fixed quality that comes on top of it, so the file is larger than the rate says. In the measured exports of a moving soft-edged shape the transparency was about 6–15 % of the video at 1080p, about 9–21 % at 720p and about 21–39 % at 640 × 360 (the higher figure at the Low tier); a smaller picture keeps its edges clean with a larger share.
- The WebM formats ask the same rates of their Opus sound, rounded to the nearest rate the Opus encoder offers.
- Audio only (M4A) uses the tier's AAC rate alone.
- Quality is greyed out for ProRes, WAV, AIFF, GIF and APNG, where the format fixes the rate.

### Bit depth

The **Bit depth** row sits under Quality. It is live only on **Audio only (WAV)** and **Audio only (AIFF)**; on every other format it is greyed out and keeps your last choice. **16-bit** is the default; **24-bit** keeps detail 16-bit cannot, which matters most for a quiet recording you are going to raise or process later. Both are rounded once from the mix, never dithered. ProRes's sound stays 16-bit. The choice is remembered with the rest of the sheet and stored in presets.

### Stems

The **Stems** row sits under Bit depth. It is live only on **Audio only (M4A)**, **Audio only (WAV)** and **Audio only (AIFF)**; on every other format it is greyed out and keeps your last choice. With a choice other than **None**, the export writes the mix and, beside it, one file per stem, in the same format, for mixing or mastering in another editor.

- **One per Track** writes one stem for each track you can hear.
- **One per Track Name** writes one stem for each track name: tracks whose names match, ignoring case and spaces at either end, share one file, named the way the first of them is spelled. A track with no name gets its own.
- A muted track has no stem, and while any track is soloed only the soloed tracks have one. A track with no sound on it (only pictures, or nothing) has none. If no track can be heard, the export is refused: "stems: no track is heard, so there is no stem to write".
- A stem is named after the mix and its track: exporting `Mix.wav` writes `Mix - Dialogue.wav` and `Mix - Music.wav`. A track with no name is called by its header's label, `Track 3`. A `/` or `:` in a track name is written as `-`, and a second stem whose name an earlier one already has, ignoring case, gets its track's label after it: `vo (Track 2)`. If an earlier stem already has that name too, a count follows the label, `vo (Track 2, 2)`, so no two stems share a file.
- **An existing file at a stem's name is replaced without asking.** The save panel asks only about the mix. The one exception: if a stem's file would be one of the project's own media files, the export stops before writing any stem, with "The stem “Mix - Dialogue.wav” would replace media this project uses; export under another name."
- Each stem holds its tracks' sound exactly as the mix plays it, with the clips' and tracks' volume, pan, fades, ducking and effects, and a track's own compressor and limiter, but **before the master**: no loudness target is applied to it and the master limiter does not touch it. So the stems added together are the mix, to within the last bit, wherever the master neither raised the level nor limited a peak. A stem can therefore peak higher than the mix; it is clipped only at full scale.
- The stems are written one after another after the mix, and the progress bar counts them. The finish line reads "Exported “Mix.wav” and 3 stems.", and the footnote under the sheet says "3 stems". The loudness figures are the mix's. Cancelling, or a failure part-way, removes the mix and every stem already written.

### Loudness

Loudness normalises the whole mix to an integrated loudness target, measured to ITU-R BS.1770-4.

| Choice | Target |
|---|---|
| **Off** | No normalisation. The export still measures its sound and reports it. |
| **−14 LUFS (streaming)** | Where the main streaming services normalise. |
| **−16 LUFS** | The usual target for stereo podcasts. |
| **−23 LUFS (broadcast)** | EBU R 128 broadcast delivery. |
| **Custom…** | Type any target from −70 to 0 LUFS, to one decimal place. |

How normalisation works:

- The export measures the real mix first. The progress line reads "Measuring loudness…" during this pass.
- It then applies **one gain** to everything. Levels inside the timeline keep their relationship to each other.
- The gain is worked out through the export's master limiter (below), so the file lands on the target even when its loudest peaks would pass the ceiling: those peaks are turned down instead of the whole mix. Only a target more than 40 dB above the mix falls short.

**Every export with sound goes through a master limiter**, normalised or not. It keeps the file's true peak under **−1 dBTP**: a mix that would pass that, from loud clips, a crossfade between two loud clips, a nest turned up or an action that raises a clip's volume, is limited instead of clipped. Sound under the ceiling passes through untouched, sample for sample. The limiter looks 3.3 ms ahead, and the export takes that back, so the sound stays exactly in sync with the picture. The preview has no master limiter: what you hear while editing is the mix before it.

A track's own compressor and limiter ([Audio](audio.md#track-compressor-and-limiter)) run before the master, on that track's sound alone, exactly as set: the export plays each such track on its own through them and mixes the tracks afterwards. The measurement for a loudness target hears them too, so the file still lands on the target. The master is only the loudness gain and this limiter; there is no master compressor or EQ. To compress the whole mix, nest everything onto one track and give that track a compressor.

The sheet fixes the ceiling at −1 dBTP. An agent can choose another (see [For agents](#for-agents)). Loudness is greyed out for GIF and APNG.

For per-clip levels, fades and Normalize, see [Audio](audio.md).

### Range

**Whole project** writes the whole timeline. **In/out range** writes only the range set on the timeline (see [Timeline](timeline.md)), snapped to the export's frame grid. The popup is greyed out when there is no range.

Inside a nest, the popup is greyed out even when the nest has a range, and its tooltip says why: an export writes the whole timeline, so it cannot use a range that belongs to the nest. Leave the nest (⌘↑) and set the range on the timeline.

### Burn in timecode

**Burn in timecode** writes the project's timecode into the exported picture, centred near the bottom and on top of everything, including captions. It appears only in the exported file, never in the preview.

- It uses the document's own timecode format, `HH:MM:SS:FF` or `HH:MM:SS.mmm`, non-drop, as the toolbar shows it.
- It shows **project time**. A file exported from an in/out range that starts at 00:00:10:00 begins at 00:00, but its first frame reads 00:00:10:00. That is the number a reviewer's note needs.

Greyed out for the audio-only formats.

## Presets

A preset stores the **choices** on the card: the format, size row or custom size, frame rate, quality tier, loudness, range and burn-in. It does not store the numbers they resolve to. A preset saved on a 1080p document that says "4K, High" exports at the right 4K size and rate on any other document.

- **Apply a preset:** pick it from the **Preset** popup. Every control is set exactly as if you had clicked it.
- **Save a preset:** click the gear and choose **Save…**, type a name and click **Save**. The name field starts with the name of the preset now chosen. Saving under a name that already exists (ignoring case) replaces that preset. The name "Custom" is reserved. While the card has an error, for example an empty custom field, **Save…** beeps and saves nothing.
- **Delete a preset:** choose it in the popup, then choose **Delete** from the gear. Delete is available only while a saved preset is chosen, and it asks no confirmation. The controls keep the preset's values, so **Save…** under the same name puts it back.
- **Change a preset:** apply it, adjust the controls, and save again under the same name. There is no separate rename.

Changing any control by hand puts the popup back on **Custom**. The popup also opens on Custom each time, even when the remembered choices happen to match a preset.

Presets are kept for your whole account in `~/Library/Application Support/Frame Job/ExportPresets.json`, so every project and window shares them. The **Dynamic Range** choice is not stored in a preset or in the remembered choices.

## Writing the file

The sheet has three buttons:

- **Cancel** closes the sheet. Nothing is written and nothing is remembered.
- **Export…** opens a save panel, then writes the file behind a progress sheet.
- **Add to Queue** opens the same save panel, then puts the job in the Export Queue so you can keep editing.

Both are greyed out while the sheet cannot work out a valid file, for example when a custom field is empty. The readout then says what to fix.

The save panel suggests the project's name with the format's extension (`Board v1.2.mp4`). It says what is being written: "Export the timeline as a movie.", "Export the timeline as an animated GIF." or "Export the timeline's audio."

### The progress sheet

**Exporting** shows a progress bar and a percentage. The status line reads "Preparing “*name*”…", then "Measuring loudness…" while the sound is measured, then "Writing “*name*”…".

- **Cancel** stops the export ("Stopping…") and removes the half-written file.
- When it finishes, the line reads "Exported “*name*”." followed by what the sound measured, for example `Peak −1.0 dBTP · −14.0 LUFS`. **Show in Finder** reveals the file, and **Close** dismisses the sheet.
- If a graphic warned while the file was drawn, the line adds a count ("1 graphic warning"), and the tooltip lists each warning with its frame.
- If a clip's cursor file could not be drawn, the clip is written without its pointer, the line adds a count after the graphic one ("1 cursor warning"), and the tooltip lists each one ("The cursor of media 3 is not drawn: …").
- A failure shows its reason on the sheet, and **Close** dismisses it.

### What the loudness line means

| Line | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `Peak −1.0 dBTP · −14.0 LUFS` | The true peak and integrated loudness of the file. |
| `Peak … · loudness not measurable` | The sound is too short or too quiet to have a loudness. |
| `Silent` | The sound is digital silence. |
| `… · peaks limited by 8.6 dB` | The master limiter turned the loudest peak down by that much to hold the ceiling. A large figure on music can be audible; turn the clips down, or ask for a lower target. |

## The Export Queue

**Window ▸ Export Queue** lists queued exports. It opens on its own whenever you click **Add to Queue**.

- Jobs run **one at a time**, in the order they were added, while you keep editing.
- An **AV1** or **VP9** job also waits for memory. These formats are encoded in software and use a lot of it: about 1.2–2.4 GB at 1080p and 4.4–8.1 GB at 4K for AV1, depending on Speed, and about 0.4–0.5 GB at 1080p and 1.1–1.6 GB at 4K for VP9. All AV1 and VP9 exports running in Frame Job at once, from the queue and from **Export…** progress sheets, may use up to a quarter of the Mac's memory together. A queued AV1 or VP9 job that would go over waits until enough of them finish, and its row says why. The row's status is one line and ends in "…" where the sentence does not fit, which at most window widths is before the figures; hold the pointer over the row and its tooltip ends with the whole sentence: "Waiting for memory: AV1 and VP9 exports running now hold about 2.3 GB of the 4.0 GB this Mac allows them, and this one needs about 2.2 GB." While it waits, a later job that fits runs first. When nothing else is running, a job always starts, however large. An **Export…** sheet never waits: it is counted, and starts straight away.
- A job holds the timeline **as it was when you confirmed it**, including its media files, reversed clips and graphics. Edits, undos, relinks and even closing the document afterwards do not change what it writes.

208	/// The size whose short edge is `short`, in the aspect of a `width` ×
209	/// `height` document: the long edge is `short` × the document's long edge
210	/// over its short one, rounded to the nearest even integer with a tie
211	/// going up, on the axis the document is longer along. A square document
212	/// gives `short` × `short`.
213	fn fitted((width, height): (u32, u32), short: u32) -> (u32, u32) {
214	    let doc_long = u64::from(width.max(height));
215	    // `validate` refuses a zero edge; the `max` keeps the division total
216	    // regardless, since no input may panic.
217	    let doc_short = u64::from(width.min(height)).max(1);
218	
219	    // The nearest even integer to short × doc_long / doc_short is twice
220	    // the nearest integer to half of it, and round(a / b) with a tie going
221	    // up is (2a + b) / 2b in integer division — here a = short × doc_long
222	    // and b = 2 × doc_short, so the whole thing is one division. u64
223	    // because a canvas need only be non-zero (`validate`), not inside
224	    // `set_canvas`'s 16..16384, so the product is not bounded by u32.
225	    let half = (u64::from(short) * doc_long + doc_short) / (2 * doc_short);
226	    // A canvas far outside those bounds can carry a ratio no u32 holds;
227	    // the row is then unusable, but a query must answer, and evenly.
228	    let long = u32::try_from(half * 2).unwrap_or(u32::MAX - 1);
229	
230	    if width >= height {
231	        (long, short)
232	    } else {
233	        (short, long)
234	    }
235	}

237	/// A size as a row that needs even dimensions writes it (spec §11 G-33),
238	/// each edge on its own: below 2 it is 2, an odd edge is one SMALLER, and an
239	/// even edge is itself. The rule `export_settings` and
240	/// [`Project::export_sizes`] share, so the list and the resolver cannot
241	/// disagree about what an H.264 will measure; the module doc says why down.
242	/// It is `ExporterWriter.evenDimension`'s arithmetic, which stays as the
243	/// floor under any caller that did not come through here.
244	pub(crate) fn even_size((width, height): (u32, u32)) -> (u32, u32) {
245	    let even = |edge: u32| if edge < 2 { 2 } else { edge - edge % 2 };
246	    (even(width), even(height))
247	}

249	/// A `width` × `height` canvas fitted inside a box: the canvas itself when
250	/// it already fits — never upscaled — and otherwise scaled down, aspect
251	/// kept, so that the edge which meets the box first takes the box's value
252	/// exactly and the other is the scaled value rounded UP to a whole pixel.
253	/// The rule an image format's size means (module doc), shared by
254	/// `export_settings` and [`Project::export_sizes`] so the two cannot
255	/// disagree about what a GIF will measure.
256	///
257	/// Up rather than to the nearest, so that the fit is its own fixed point.
258	/// Fitting the result again compares box × canvas products on the two
259	/// axes, and the derived edge — never below its exact value — keeps the
260	/// same axis limiting, whose derived edge is the same ceiling; rounded to
261	/// the nearest it can fall below the exact value, flip the limiting axis
262	/// on the second pass, and take a pixel off the other edge (a 3024 × 1964
263	/// recording's 1080p box, 1662 × 1080, came back 1662 × 1079 and then
264	/// 1661 × 1079). The ceiling never leaves the box: the limiting axis is
265	/// the one whose exact scaled value fits, and a whole number no smaller
266	/// than a value that fits inside a whole box edge fits too.
267	pub(crate) fn fit_within((width, height): (u32, u32), (box_w, box_h): (u32, u32)) -> (u32, u32) {
268	    if width <= box_w && height <= box_h {
269	        return (width, height);
270	    }
271	    let (w, h) = (u64::from(width).max(1), u64::from(height).max(1));
272	    let (bw, bh) = (u64::from(box_w).max(1), u64::from(box_h).max(1));
273	    // The width meets the box first when box_w / w ≤ box_h / h, which is
274	    // box_w × h ≤ box_h × w with no division to round.
275	    let (fw, fh) = if bw * h <= bh * w {
276	        (bw, ceil_div(h * bw, w))
277	    } else {
278	        (ceil_div(w * bh, h), bh)
279	    };
280	    let edge = |value: u64| u32::try_from(value).unwrap_or(u32::MAX).max(1);
281	    (edge(fw), edge(fh))
282	}

284	/// `a / b` rounded up to a whole number; `b ≥ 1`.
285	fn ceil_div(a: u64, b: u64) -> u64 {
286	    a.div_ceil(b)
287	}

14	//! The output sizes the export sheet offers for one document and one
15	//! format — `rc_export_sizes` (spec §7.8) — and the one rule for what a
16	//! size MEANS on an image format, which `export_settings` applies too.
17	//!
18	//! A preset is an encoding and carries no size (`export.rs`), so the size
19	//! is a second choice, and this module is the list that choice is made
20	//! from: the format's cap if it has one, the document's own size, and the
21	//! standard sizes fitted to the document's aspect. The FIRST row is the
22	//! default — the rule every list the export sheet is built from follows —
23	//! which is the document's size for a movie format and the cap for an
24	//! image format, because an image format's cap is the point of the row
25	//! and not a ceiling that only applies from above.
26	//!
27	//! **The number is the short edge.** A standard size is named by one
28	//! number, and the number people use is the short one: "1080p ultrawide"
29	//! is 2560 × 1080 and "1080p vertical" is 1080 × 1920, and both are 1080p
30	//! to everyone who says it. Naming by the long edge would call the
31	//! ultrawide 2560p and the vertical 1920p, which nobody does. So a row
32	//! keeps its short edge exactly and the long edge follows the document:
33	//! L = S × long / short of the document, on whichever axis the document is
34	//! longer along, and S × S for a square.
35	//!
36	//! **The long edge is rounded to even.** 4:2:0 chroma puts one colour
37	//! sample under each 2 × 2 block of luma, so H.264 and HEVC want even
38	//! dimensions, and `ExporterWriter.evenDimension` rounds an odd one down
39	//! before writing. Rounding here — to the nearest even integer, a tie
40	//! going up — means the size the popup shows is the size the file has;
41	//! leaving it to the writer would change the size behind the sheet's
42	//! back.
43	//!
44	//! **The even rule (spec §11 G-33).** The same is true of the document row
45	//! and of any size asked for, so on every row that needs even dimensions
46	//! (`Preset::even_sized`: every row AVFoundation writes but ProRes 4444)
47	//! the size is resolved HERE, by [`even_size`]: the document row's numbers
48	//! in this list, and in `export_settings` whatever was asked. An odd edge
49	//! is one pixel SMALLER. Down, because that is the size the writer already
50	//! wrote, so the report moves to the file and no file changes size;
51	//! because rounding up would hand the encoder a frame larger than the
52	//! picture on that axis; and because every listed row is then its own
53	//! fixed point, as an image format's is. The row is named "Document
54	//! (even)" when its numbers are not the canvas's, which is the whole of
55	//! how the popup says why. The argument this replaces was that a "Document
56	//! size" that was not the document's size would be a lie; the lie was the
57	//! row that said 321 × 181 over a file of 320 × 180. ProRes 4444 and the
58	//! two image formats keep an odd edge, and their row is "Document size",
59	//! the canvas as it is.
60	//!
61	//! **An image format's numbers are the file's.** A GIF or an APNG is
62	//! written frame by frame with the picture FITTED inside the size — aspect
63	//! kept, never upscaled — where a movie is letterboxed to exactly the frame
64	//! asked for (`ExporterImageSequence`, spec §7.8): padding costs bytes in
65	//! every frame for pixels that carry nothing, and a bigger frame carries no
66	//! more detail. So on those two formats every row here, and every size
67	//! `export_settings` resolves — the cap, a standard row, a custom size — is
68	//! the canvas fitted inside that box ([`fit_within`]), so that the popup,
69	//! the sheet's readout and the `export` tool all report the numbers the
70	//! file will have: a vertical 1080 × 1920 timeline's "GIF default" is
71	//! 152 × 270, not 480 × 270. The fit is decided here, once; the writer
72	//! draws each frame at exactly this size and does not fit a second time.
73	//! It is also its own fixed point — a fitted size fed back as the box
74	//! fits to itself — because that is exactly what happens: the sheet and
75	//! the tool send a listed row's numbers back through `export_settings` as
76	//! `width` and `height`, and a fit that could move a derived edge by a
77	//! pixel on the second pass would show one size and write another.
78	//!
79	//! **Rows may repeat.** A 1920 × 1080 document's 1080p row IS the document
80	//! row, and on a 1080 × 1920 document every image-format row from 1080p up
81	//! is the document again. They are listed anyway, because an id is the
82	//! `export` tool's vocabulary and a request for `1080p` has to mean the
83	//! same thing on every document — refusing it exactly where it is a no-op
84	//! would be the popup's tidiness leaking into an API. The sheet hides a
85	//! row whose numbers an earlier row already has, so a person never sees one
86	//! size under two names, and the row that shows is the one whose name says
87	//! more ("Document size" over "1080p"). Rows larger than the document are
88	//! offered for a movie — they were before, as the 4K preset — because a
89	//! 720p screen recording exported at 4K for a platform that picks its
90	//! bitrate by resolution is a real request.

97	/// The standard sizes, largest first, as (id, name, short edge). The id is
98	/// the `export` tool's vocabulary and the name is the popup's; they differ
99	/// only for 4K, which nobody calls 2160p out loud but which needs a
100	/// short-edge id to sit in the same vocabulary as the other three.
101	const STANDARD: [(&str, &str, u32); 4] = [
102	    ("2160p", "4K", 2160),
103	    ("1440p", "1440p", 1440),
104	    ("1080p", "1080p", 1080),

128	    /// The sizes the export sheet offers for `preset_id` against this
129	    /// document, as the JSON array of `{id, name, width, height}` rows
130	    /// `rc_export_sizes` returns, in menu order — the first is the default.
131	    ///
132	    /// The rows:
133	    ///
134	    /// 1. `preset` — the format's cap, "GIF default" / "APNG default", for
135	    ///    the two rows of the table that carry one; nothing for the rest.
136	    /// 2. `document` — "Document size", the canvas as it is; on a row that
137	    ///    needs even dimensions the canvas evened ([`even_size`]), named
138	    ///    "Document (even)" when that is not the canvas's own size.
139	    /// 3. `2160p` ("4K"), `1440p`, `1080p`, `720p` — the short edge named,

141	    ///
142	    /// On an image format every row's numbers are the canvas fitted inside
143	    /// that row's box, never upscaled — the size the file will have. Rows
144	    /// may repeat an earlier row's numbers and are listed anyway (the
145	    /// module doc says why); the sheet hides the repeats.
146	    ///
147	    /// One list for every movie format, the audio-only row included: a
148	    /// width is reported for it the way `export_settings` reports one, and
149	    /// the sheet disables the control rather than this module keeping a
150	    /// second rule for one row. `Err` for an unknown preset, naming it —
151	    /// the same lookup and the same words as `export_settings`.
152	    pub fn export_sizes(&self, preset_id: &str) -> Result<Value, String> {
153	        let preset = export::preset(preset_id)?;
154	        let document = (self.canvas.width, self.canvas.height);
155	        let fits = preset.fits_inside_size();
156	        let sized = |(width, height): (u32, u32)| {
157	            if fits {
158	                fit_within(document, (width, height))
159	            } else {
160	                (width, height)
161	            }
162	        };

164	        let mut rows: Vec<Row> = Vec::new();
165	        if let Some(cap) = preset.size {
166	            // The codec in capitals is the format's name as people write
167	            // it — GIF, APNG — for the two rows that carry a cap.
168	            let (width, height) = sized(cap);
169	            rows.push(Row {
170	                id: "preset",
171	                name: format!("{} default", preset.codec.to_uppercase()),
172	                width,
173	                height,
174	            });
175	        }
176	        // The id is `document` either way: the name is the popup's, and it
177	        // changes only when the numbers are not the canvas's.
178	        let listed = if preset.even_sized() {
179	            even_size(document)
180	        } else {
181	            document
182	        };
183	        let name = if listed == document {
184	            "Document size"
185	        } else {
186	            "Document (even)"
187	        };
188	        rows.push(Row {
189	            id: "document",
190	            name: name.to_string(),
191	            width: listed.0,
192	            height: listed.1,
193	        });
194	        for (id, name, short) in STANDARD {
195	            let (width, height) = sized(fitted(document, short));
196	            rows.push(Row {
197	                id,
198	                name: name.to_string(),
199	                width,
200	                height,
201	            });
202	        }

208	/// The size whose short edge is `short`, in the aspect of a `width` ×
209	/// `height` document: the long edge is `short` × the document's long edge
210	/// over its short one, rounded to the nearest even integer with a tie
211	/// going up, on the axis the document is longer along. A square document
212	/// gives `short` × `short`.
213	fn fitted((width, height): (u32, u32), short: u32) -> (u32, u32) {
214	    let doc_long = u64::from(width.max(height));
215	    // `validate` refuses a zero edge; the `max` keeps the division total
216	    // regardless, since no input may panic.
217	    let doc_short = u64::from(width.min(height)).max(1);
218	
219	    // The nearest even integer to short × doc_long / doc_short is twice
220	    // the nearest integer to half of it, and round(a / b) with a tie going
221	    // up is (2a + b) / 2b in integer division — here a = short × doc_long
222	    // and b = 2 × doc_short, so the whole thing is one division. u64
223	    // because a canvas need only be non-zero (`validate`), not inside
224	    // `set_canvas`'s 16..16384, so the product is not bounded by u32.
225	    let half = (u64::from(short) * doc_long + doc_short) / (2 * doc_short);
226	    // A canvas far outside those bounds can carry a ratio no u32 holds;
227	    // the row is then unusable, but a query must answer, and evenly.
228	    let long = u32::try_from(half * 2).unwrap_or(u32::MAX - 1);
229	
230	    if width >= height {
231	        (long, short)
232	    } else {
233	        (short, long)
234	    }
235	}
236	
237	/// A size as a row that needs even dimensions writes it (spec §11 G-33),
238	/// each edge on its own: below 2 it is 2, an odd edge is one SMALLER, and an
239	/// even edge is itself. The rule `export_settings` and
240	/// [`Project::export_sizes`] share, so the list and the resolver cannot
241	/// disagree about what an H.264 will measure; the module doc says why down.
242	/// It is `ExporterWriter.evenDimension`'s arithmetic, which stays as the
243	/// floor under any caller that did not come through here.
244	pub(crate) fn even_size((width, height): (u32, u32)) -> (u32, u32) {
245	    let even = |edge: u32| if edge < 2 { 2 } else { edge - edge % 2 };
246	    (even(width), even(height))
247	}
248	
249	/// A `width` × `height` canvas fitted inside a box: the canvas itself when
250	/// it already fits — never upscaled — and otherwise scaled down, aspect
251	/// kept, so that the edge which meets the box first takes the box's value
252	/// exactly and the other is the scaled value rounded UP to a whole pixel.
253	/// The rule an image format's size means (module doc), shared by
254	/// `export_settings` and [`Project::export_sizes`] so the two cannot
255	/// disagree about what a GIF will measure.
256	///
257	/// Up rather than to the nearest, so that the fit is its own fixed point.
258	/// Fitting the result again compares box × canvas products on the two
259	/// axes, and the derived edge — never below its exact value — keeps the
260	/// same axis limiting, whose derived edge is the same ceiling; rounded to
261	/// the nearest it can fall below the exact value, flip the limiting axis
262	/// on the second pass, and take a pixel off the other edge (a 3024 × 1964
263	/// recording's 1080p box, 1662 × 1080, came back 1662 × 1079 and then
264	/// 1661 × 1079). The ceiling never leaves the box: the limiting axis is
265	/// the one whose exact scaled value fits, and a whole number no smaller
266	/// than a value that fits inside a whole box edge fits too.
267	pub(crate) fn fit_within((width, height): (u32, u32), (box_w, box_h): (u32, u32)) -> (u32, u32) {
268	    if width <= box_w && height <= box_h {
269	        return (width, height);
270	    }
271	    let (w, h) = (u64::from(width).max(1), u64::from(height).max(1));
272	    let (bw, bh) = (u64::from(box_w).max(1), u64::from(box_h).max(1));
273	    // The width meets the box first when box_w / w ≤ box_h / h, which is
274	    // box_w × h ≤ box_h × w with no division to round.
275	    let (fw, fh) = if bw * h <= bh * w {
276	        (bw, ceil_div(h * bw, w))
277	    } else {
278	        (ceil_div(w * bh, h), bh)
279	    };
280	    let edge = |value: u64| u32::try_from(value).unwrap_or(u32::MAX).max(1);
281	    (edge(fw), edge(fh))
282	}
283	
284	/// `a / b` rounded up to a whole number; `b ≥ 1`.
285	fn ceil_div(a: u64, b: u64) -> u64 {
286	    a.div_ceil(b)
287	}

377	    /// One row of the Quality popup: a video rate expressed as bits per pixel

382	    /// recommended upload for 1080p SDR H.264 at 30 fps is 8 Mbps, and
383	    /// 1920 × 1080 × 30 is 62.2 Mpixel/s, so "High" is 8 000 000 / 62 200 000

385	    /// 0.75× and 1.5× of it — 4, 6 and 12 Mbps at 1080p30, which brackets

394	    /// what choosing "High" ought to mean.
395	    struct QualityTier {
396	        let name: String
397	        /// Bits per pixel per frame, for H.264 at 30 fps or less.
398	        let bitsPerPixel: Double
399	        /// AAC-LC stereo, bits per second. 128 kbps is the streaming
400	        /// baseline, 256 is what Apple Music ships, and 320 is where AAC-LC
401	        /// stops paying for the extra bits.
402	        let audioBitsPerSecond: Int
403	
404	        /// The video rate for a `width` × `height` frame at `fps`.
405	        ///
406	        /// The 30 is not a stand-in for `fps`: the frame rate enters through
407	        /// `rateFactor` instead, because bits do not scale linearly with it.
408	        /// Consecutive frames are more alike the closer together they are,
409	        /// which is why YouTube's ladder asks 1.5× for its 48–60 fps column
410	        /// and nothing extra for 24 fps over 30. This mirrors that shape —
411	        /// one step at 30 and below, one above it.
412	        func videoBitsPerSecond(width: Int, height: Int, fps: Fps, codec: String) -> Int {
413	            let pixels = Double(max(width, 1)) * Double(max(height, 1))
414	            let rateFactor = fps.double > 30.5 ? 1.5 : 1.0
415	            // HEVC reaches the same picture at roughly 60 % of H.264's rate —
416	            // the ratio between the two 1080p rungs of the same Apple
417	            // specification the tiers are calibrated against. AV1 takes
418	            // HEVC's factor (spec §11 CX-9 (2)): its efficiency goes to the
419	            // picture, not the file size. VP9 takes it too (CX-9 (2), CX-16 (7)).
420	            let lower = codec.lowercased()

423	            let bits = pixels * 30 * bitsPerPixel * rateFactor * codecFactor
424	            // To the nearest 100 kbps: these are estimates, and a request for
425	            // "7 963 200 bits" would claim a precision they do not have.
426	            return max(100_000, Int((bits / 100_000).rounded()) * 100_000)
427	        }

429	        private static func isHEVC(_ codec: String) -> Bool {
430	            let codec = codec.lowercased()

433	    }

437	    /// session's ladder when it carries none.

440	        QualityTier(name: "Medium", bitsPerPixel: 0.096, audioBitsPerSecond: 192_000),

442	        QualityTier(name: "Maximum", bitsPerPixel: 0.193, audioBitsPerSecond: 320_000),

57	/// The export sheet's ANSWER half: read the controls, ask the core what they
58	/// describe, and repaint the card from what it said.
59	///
60	/// The seam is the §7 rule the sheet is built on, drawn as a file boundary.
61	/// `ExportSheetController.swift` owns the controls — it makes the popups and
62	/// the fields, lists the sizes, and hands a person something to choose with.
63	/// Nothing there decides an output size, a rate or a duration, because
64	/// nothing in this dialog does: every number the card shows comes back from
65	/// `rc_export_settings`, and this file is the whole of the round trip. It
66	/// turns a selection into the override object the core reads (`overrides()`),
67	/// sends it (`resolve()`), and writes the answer into the readout, the
68	/// footnote and the controls' enablement (`syncReadout()`). Between those
69	/// three, the `current…` accessors are the one place a popup index becomes a
70	/// meaning, so a control's index arithmetic is never spelled twice.
71	///
72	/// The one number the sheet DOES choose is the bit rate, and it is here for
73	/// that reason rather than beside the Quality popup: a tier is a REQUEST
74	/// (`ExportSheetOptions.swift` holds the ladder), and turning one into bits
75	/// per second needs the frame the controls are asking for — which is
76	/// `requestedFormat()`, three accessors deep into this file and nowhere near
77	/// the popup.
78	///
79	/// The cut is the size payment `ExportSheetController.swift` owed at 1114
80	/// lines against app/CLAUDE.md's ~600 cap, and it is a pure move: the same
81	/// methods, in the same order, with the same bodies. **The toll is
82	/// visibility**, for the reason `ExporterLoudness.swift` records — `private`
83	/// on an extension member reaches only its own file, and a stored property
84	/// cannot live in an extension at all. So every control, every field and
85	/// every piece of state this file reads is internal in the file that
86	/// declares it, and the four members the controls call back into —
87	/// `resolve()`, `currentPreset`, `isCustomSize` and `isCustomLoudness` — are
88	/// internal here. Everything else below stays `private`, because a `private`
89	/// extension member is reachable from the rest of THIS file, and nothing
90	/// outside it has ever asked.
91	/// Phase 7 added the OTHER direction to this file, and it belongs here for the
92	/// same reason the first one does: `currentChoice` is a reading of the
93	/// controls, exactly as `overrides()` is, and `apply(_:)` is that reading run
94	/// backwards. Keeping the pair together is what makes a saved preset and the
95	/// remembered choice provably the same thing as clicking each control by hand —
96	/// there is one account of what a stored choice means, and both halves of it
97	/// are on one screen.
98	extension ExportSheetController {
99	
100	    // MARK: - Resolving
101	
102	    /// Asks the core for the settings the current controls describe, then
103	    /// repaints the readout from the answer.
104	    ///
105	    /// A refusal is not an error dialog: the message goes in the readout and
106	    /// Export greys out, so a bad override reads as "this combination is not
107	    /// available" rather than interrupting the person adjusting it.
108	    func resolve() {
109	        guard let project = editor?.document?.project, let preset = currentPreset else {
110	            resolved = nil
111	            resolveError = "This build has no export presets."
112	            syncReadout()
113	            return
114	        }
115	        // A format whose sizes the core could not list is not exported at
116	        // all, whatever the settings call would answer: the one refusal
117	        // `rc_export_sizes` shares with `rc_export_settings` is an unknown
118	        // preset, but a listing can also fail on its own (a reply this
119	        // build cannot decode), and the size the sheet would then send is
120	        // the fields' clamped floor, 16 × 16, which nobody asked for.
121	        if let message = sizesError {
122	            resolved = nil
123	            resolveError = message
124	            syncReadout()
125	            return
126	        }
127	        // An empty Custom field is not a size. Its formatter accepts the
128	        // empty string as "no value", `integerValue` reads that as 0, and
129	        // the clamp would turn it into the 16-pixel floor — an export
130	        // nobody asked for, reached by clearing a field and clicking
131	        // Export…, since that click commits the field before it reads.
132	        if isCustomSize, currentApplies.size,
133	            widthField.stringValue.isEmpty || heightField.stringValue.isEmpty
134	        {
135	            resolved = nil
136	            resolveError = "Type a width and a height, or pick a size from the list."
137	            syncReadout()
138	            return
139	        }
140	        // The same rule for the Custom loudness field, and for the same
141	        // reason: an empty field is not a target, and reading it as one would
142	        // export at whatever the clamp's floor happens to be.
143	        if isCustomLoudness, currentApplies.loudness, loudnessField.stringValue.isEmpty {
144	            resolved = nil
145	            resolveError = "Type a loudness target in LUFS, or pick one from the list."
146	            syncReadout()
147	            return
148	        }
149	        do {
150	            resolved = try ReelExport.settings(
151	                project, preset: preset.id, overrides: overrides())
152	            resolveError = nil
153	        } catch {
154	            resolved = nil
155	            resolveError = error.localizedDescription
156	        }
157	        syncReadout()
158	    }
159	
160	    // MARK: - The card as a value
161	
162	    /// The controls as an `ExportChoice`, with the sheet's own gating applied:
163	    /// a control the chosen format cannot take (`Applies`) contributes
164	    /// nothing, exactly as it contributes no override. So a preset saved off
165	    /// an audio-only row carries no size, and one saved off a GIF carries no
166	    /// loudness — the record says what was actually asked for and never what
167	    /// a greyed-out popup happened to be sitting on.
168	    ///
169	    /// **The burn-in is gated by that same rule and used not to be**, which
170	    /// broke the sentence above rather than any of the core's: a tick made on
171	    /// an H.264 row and carried across to WAV was written into the record
172	    /// beside a size, an fps and a tier all three deliberately left empty, so
173	    /// a named preset — and the remembered choice, which is this same
174	    /// value — said a file with no picture would carry a burn-in. It is not an
175	    /// override, so nothing downstream ever refused it; `Applies.burnIn`
176	    /// (below) is where it is refused now.
177	    ///
178	    /// The `name` is empty: naming a choice is the Save… item's business.
179	    var currentChoice: ExportChoice {
180	        var choice = ExportChoice(presetID: currentPreset?.id ?? "")
181	        if currentApplies.size {
182	            if isCustomSize {
183	                choice.customSize = [clampedSize(widthField), clampedSize(heightField)]
184	            } else {
185	                let index = sizePopup.indexOfSelectedItem
186	                // The ROW's id, never its index (`ExportChoice.sizeRow`).
187	                // Index 0 is recorded like any other: it is a row a person
188	                // chose, and `sizeOverride()`'s decision to send it as no
189	                // override at all is about the CORE's default and not about
190	                // what the popup was showing.
191	                if index >= 0, index < visibleSizes.count {
192	                    choice.sizeRow = visibleSizes[index].id
193	                }
194	            }
195	        }
196	        choice.fps = currentRate.map { [$0.num, $0.den] }
197	        choice.qualityTier = currentTier?.name
198	        choice.loudness = currentLoudness
199	        choice.inOutRange = rangePopup.indexOfSelectedItem == 1
200	        choice.burnInTimecode = currentApplies.burnIn && recipeOptions.burnInTimecode
201	        choice.encoderSpeed = encoderSpeedChoice.rawValue
202	        choice.audioBits = audioBitsChoice
203	        choice.stems = stemsChoice
204	        return choice
205	    }
206	
207	    /// Writes a stored choice back into the controls. **The order is
208	    /// load-bearing and this method is where it is written down**; every
209	    /// caller — the remembered choice in `loadView`, a preset picked from the
210	    /// popup — goes through here so there is only ever one order.
211	    ///
212	    /// 1. **Format FIRST, before the sizes are listed.** A programmatic
213	    ///    `selectItem` sends no action, so `formatChanged`'s `sizesPreset`
214	    ///    guard never fires and nothing rebuilds on its own; listing after the
215	    ///    pick is what makes the rows this format's rows.
216	    /// 2. **Size AFTER `rebuildSizes()`**, which ends with an unconditional
217	    ///    `sizePopup.selectItem(at: 0)` and would undo a selection made before
218	    ///    it.
219	    /// 3. **A custom LOUDNESS selects "Custom…" first and fills the field
220	    ///    second**, because `syncReadout` overwrites that field from the popup
221	    ///    whenever the popup is not on Custom — and `resolve()` runs one
222	    ///    `syncReadout` after this returns.
223	    /// 4. **`in_out` degrades to "Whole project"** on a document that has no
224	    ///    range: the popup only carries that row when `range != nil`, so
225	    ///    selecting index 1 would select nothing at all.
226	    ///
227	    /// It does NOT resolve. The caller does, once, after the last control has
228	    /// moved — a resolve per control would be six FFI round trips to paint one
229	    /// card.
230	    func apply(_ choice: ExportChoice) {
231	        if let index = presets.firstIndex(where: { $0.id == choice.presetID }) {
232	            formatPopup.selectItem(at: index)
233	        }
234	        rebuildSizes()
235	        applySize(choice)
236	
237	        if let fps = choice.fps, fps.count == 2,
238	            let index = Self.rates.firstIndex(where: { $0.num == fps[0] && $0.den == fps[1] })
239	        {
240	            ratePopup.selectItem(at: index + 1)
241	        } else {
242	            ratePopup.selectItem(at: 0)
243	        }
244	
245	        if let name = choice.qualityTier,
246	            let index = Self.tiers.firstIndex(where: { $0.name == name })
247	        {
248	            qualityPopup.selectItem(at: index + 1)
249	        } else {
250	            qualityPopup.selectItem(at: 0)
251	        }
252	
253	        applyLoudness(choice)
254	        rangePopup.selectItem(at: choice.inOutRange && range != nil ? 1 : 0)
255	        burnInCheckbox.state = choice.burnInTimecode ? .on : .off
256	        applySpeed(choice)
257	        applyAudioBits(choice)
258	        applyStems(choice)
259	    }
260	
261	    /// Step 2, after the listing. A row whose id this format does not offer —
262	    /// a GIF's cap under H.264, or a row `visibleSizes` hid because an earlier
263	    /// row already has its numbers — falls back to the SAME NUMBERS under
264	    /// whatever row does show them, and only then to the format's default.
265	    /// Hiding is a tidiness of the popup's (`visibleSizes`), so a choice of
266	    /// "1080p" on a 1920 × 1080 document has to land on "Document size" rather
267	    /// than be dropped: it is the same export.
268	    private func applySize(_ choice: ExportChoice) {
269	        if let row = choice.sizeRow {
270	            if let index = visibleSizes.firstIndex(where: { $0.id == row }) {
271	                sizePopup.selectItem(at: index)
272	                return
273	            }
274	            if let hidden = sizes.first(where: { $0.id == row }),
275	                let index = visibleSizes.firstIndex(where: {
276	                    $0.width == hidden.width && $0.height == hidden.height
277	                })
278	            {
279	                sizePopup.selectItem(at: index)
280	                return
281	            }
282	            return
283	        }
284	        guard let custom = choice.customSize, custom.count == 2 else { return }
285	        // "Custom…" is the item after the last visible row.
286	        sizePopup.selectItem(at: visibleSizes.count)
287	        widthField.integerValue = custom[0]
288	        heightField.integerValue = custom[1]
289	    }
290	
291	    /// Step 3: the row first, the field second.
292	    private func applyLoudness(_ choice: ExportChoice) {
293	        guard let target = choice.loudness else {
294	            loudnessPopup.selectItem(at: 0)
295	            return
296	        }
297	        if let index = Self.loudnessTargets.firstIndex(of: target) {
298	            loudnessPopup.selectItem(at: index + 1)
299	            return
300	        }
301	        loudnessPopup.selectItem(at: Self.loudnessTargets.count + 1)
302	        loudnessField.doubleValue = target
303	    }
304	
305	    var currentPreset: ExportPreset? {
306	        let index = formatPopup.indexOfSelectedItem
307	        guard index >= 0, index < presets.count else { return nil }
308	        return presets[index]
309	    }

312	
313	    /// True while the Size popup's last item, "Custom…", is chosen — which is
314	    /// also the state of a popup whose listing failed, since Custom is then
315	    /// its only item; harmless, because `resolve()` refuses that case before

318

320	    /// for a preset that has no frames, so a rate picked for a movie cannot
321	    /// follow the user into an audio-only export.
322	    private var currentRate: Fps? {
323	        let index = ratePopup.indexOfSelectedItem - 1
324	        guard currentApplies.frameRate, index >= 0, index < Self.rates.count else { return nil }

== peak_dbtp number None The ceiling of the master limiter every export with sound runs, in dBTP: the file's true peak stays at or under it. Omit for -1 (the sheet's fixed value); 0 is the loosest, and there is no off. Legal with or without loudness_lufs. How far the limiter turned the hottest peak down is the result's limited_db. == audio_bits integer [16, 24] audio_wav's and audio_aiff's bit depth — the sheet's Bit depth popup: 16 (the default) or 24, rounded once from the float mix, never dithered. Refused on every other preset (ProRes keeps 16). == preset string None Export preset id — one per encoding, a container and a codec with no size of its own (that is size's). h264 is what the export sheet opens on. Four rows keep a transparent canvas transparent: prores_4444, hevc_alpha and vp9_alpha_webm (the movie rows — see size, which constrains them) and apng. gif is not one of them: it can show a transparent pixel but has no alpha channel, so nothing partial survives it. prores_422, prores_4444 and hevc_10bit keep the compositor's 16-bit frames at 10 bits (ProRes 4444 at 12); h264, hevc and hevc_alpha are 8-bit. av1 is AV1 in an MP4 with AAC and av1_webm the same AV1 in a WebM with Opus, both 10-bit, encoded by the bundled SVT-AV1 at encoder_speed; Macs before M3 cannot play them back. vp9_webm is VP9 in a WebM with Opus from the bundled libvpx, at one speed: 8-bit (Profile 0) for an SDR picture, 10-bit (Profile 2) for HLG and PQ. vp9_alpha_webm is tha == dynamic_range string ['hlg', 'pq', 'sdr'] An HDR (HLG) project's picture on hevc_10bit, av1, av1_webm, vp9_webm, prores_422 and prores_4444 — the sheet's Dynamic Range popup: hlg (the default; BT.2100 HLG, no Dolby Vision), pq (HDR10: BT.2100 PQ at 1,000 cd/m², mastering display P3-D65 0.005–1,000 cd/m², MaxCLL 1,000, MaxFALL 0) or sdr (the SDR version). Every other video preset (vp9_alpha_webm too) writes the SDR version; hlg and pq are refused there and in an SDR project, where sdr changes nothing. == loudness_lufs number None Normalise the whole mix to this integrated loudness, in LUFS — the sheet's Loudness popup, whose rows are -14 (streaming), -16 (podcast) and -23 (EBU R 128 broadcast). The export measures itself first and then applies ONE gain to everything, solved through the master limiter every export runs at peak_dbtp, so the file lands on the target and its loudest peaks are limited rather than the whole mix capped. Omit not to normalise: the export still measures, still limits at the ceiling and still reports. Ignored where there is no sound to measure (gif, apng). == size ['string', 'array'] None Output size — the sheet's Size popup. # CLAUDE.md — the documentation site

The public user documentation: Astro with Starlight, one page per feature or tight family of
features. `pnpm` manages it, Node is pinned by `.node-version`. `README.md` has the commands.

## Where things are

```
astro.config.mjs        Starlight's settings: title, logo, fonts, theme, plugins
sidebar.mjs             every page's place in the navigation, in order
src/content/docs/       the pages: <section>/<page>.mdx
src/data/features.json  THE FEATURE LIST: what /features/ renders and what the proof reads
src/components/         AtAGlance (a page's facts), Shot (a screen in both looks),
                        FeatureIndex (the filterable list)
src/assets/screens/     WebP captures, written only by scripts/import-screens.mjs
src/styles/             the brand: the mark's inks, the app's faces, square chrome
```

## The rule that matters

**Every claim is written from the code.** A label, a default, a range, a shortcut, a limit or a
refusal is checked against `app/Sources/`, `core/src/`, `graphic/` or `mcp-proxy/` before it is
written, and the code wins over `docs/guide/`, a spec or an ADR. Never write what a feature
probably does. If the code cannot settle it, leave it out.

Nothing dev-only, deferred or unbuilt is documented. That excludes the dev tools (`snapshot_ui`,
`perform_menu_item`, `cancel_sheet`, `select_inspector_tab`, `play_preview`, `graphic_memory`,
`loudness_meter`, `land_recording`, `analysis_job`, `transcript_view`, `playback_rebuilds`,
`assistant_send`, `assistant_answer`) and every `-RCDev` launch default.

## Who reads this

Someone editing a video, who has never read this repository. They want to know what a thing does,
how to do it, and what will stop them. They do not care how it is built.

So a page never mentions: spec or decision IDs (`AU-12`, `§11`), road maps, phases, issue numbers,
source file or type names, `rc_*` exports, format version numbers, proofs, tests, or the history
of a feature. Internal words get translated: "refused" becomes what the user sees ("Frame Job
won't do this while…"), "the core" and "the op" disappear. A tool name is the one exception: the
MCP pages and `tools=` in `AtAGlance` name agent tools, because those are the product's interface.

## Voice

- Plain, direct and second person. Say what it does, then how. Short sentences.
- Open with what the feature is for, in a sentence or two, before any steps.
- British spelling in prose, as `docs/guide/` does (colour, centre, grey, normalise), and the
  app's exact spelling for its own labels (the **Color** tab, **Normalize**).
- Contractions are fine. No marketing: never "powerful", "seamless", "effortless", "robust",
  "simply", "just", "easily", "unleash", "supercharge".
- Prefer a full stop or a comma to an em dash.
- State defaults, ranges and limits as numbers. Say what happens at the edges, because that is
  what a reader comes to a reference for.
- No filler sections. A page with nothing to say under a heading doesn't have that heading.

## Page shape

```mdx
---

---
```
title: Audio-only exports
description: Export the timeline's sound with no picture, as a compressed M4A or an uncompressed WAV or AIFF.
---

import { Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';
import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';

Frame Job can write the timeline's sound with no picture: an M4A to send to someone, or a WAV or AIFF to hand to a mastering engineer, a DAW or a podcast editor.

<AtAGlance
  menu="File ▸ Export…"
  keys="⌘E"
  where="Export sheet ▸ Format"
  tools="export"
/>

## Export the sound

<Steps>

1. Choose **File ▸ Export…** or press <kbd>⌘E</kbd>.

2. In **Format**, choose **Audio only (M4A)**, **Audio only (WAV)** or **Audio only (AIFF)**.

3. Set the [controls that apply](#which-controls-apply). The readout shows the length in milliseconds rather than frames, for example `Audio only · 00:01:12.200`.

4. Choose **Export…** and name the file, or **Add to Queue** to keep editing while it's written.

</Steps>

## Audio only (M4A)

An `.m4a` file holding AAC sound, 48 kHz stereo. This is the one to send to someone, because it's by far the smallest.

The sound is 192 kbps unless you pick a tier in [Quality](/export/quality/): **Low** is 128 kbps, **Medium** 192, **High** 256 and **Maximum** 320. The footnote reads `AAC · M4A`, with the rate added when you pick a tier.

Chapter markers are written into the file as [chapters](/export/chapters/), and the file is written with fast start, so a player can begin before all of it has arrived.

## Audio only (WAV)

A `.wav` file of uncompressed sound, 48 kHz stereo. Choose it when the mix is going into someone else's tool, where a second round of lossy compression is the one thing you can't take back.

It's 16-bit by default, or 24-bit through [Bit depth](/export/bit-depth/). That's about 11.5 MB a minute at 16 bits and 17.3 MB a minute at 24. The footnote reads `LPCM · WAV`, with `24-bit` added at that depth.

A WAV holds no chapters, so chapter markers are left out.

## Audio only (AIFF)

The same samples as a WAV, in an `.aiff` file. WAV stores each sample little-endian and AIFF big-endian, which matters only to the software reading the file, so choose whichever your tool asks for.

Everything else is as for WAV: 48 kHz stereo, 16 or 24 bits, the same file size and no chapters. The footnote reads `LPCM · AIFF`.

## Which controls apply

A control an audio format can't use is greyed out. It keeps what it shows, and nothing from it reaches the file.

| Control | M4A | WAV and AIFF |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Quality** | Sets the AAC rate | Greyed out |
| **Bit depth** | Greyed out | 16-bit or 24-bit |
| [**Stems**](/export/stems/) | Live | Live |
| [**Loudness**](/export/loudness/) | Live | Live |
| [**Range**](/export/range/) | Live | Live |
| **Size**, **Frame rate**, **Speed**, **Burn in timecode** | Greyed out | Greyed out |

**Size** has nothing to set because there's no picture. A preset saved from an audio format stores no size, so it can't carry one over to a movie.

## The 48 kHz stereo master

Every export with sound, movies included, reads the mix once as 48 kHz stereo at 32-bit float, and rounds it once at the very end. In between, the loudness gain and the limiter both work on the float mix, so nothing has been clipped before they act.

The limiter holds the file's true peak under −1 dBTP. See [Export loudness](/export/loudness/). Sound under that ceiling passes through unchanged.

The final rounding goes to the nearest value at the file's bit depth, with no dither at 16 or 24 bits.

There's no control for the sample rate or the channel count. Whatever your sources are, the file is 48 kHz stereo.

## Good to know

- An audio export writes the whole timeline's mix, or its in/out range. Hidden picture doesn't change it, and a muted track stays silent.
- A timeline with no sound at all can't be exported as audio. The export stops with "There is nothing on the timeline to export — add a clip first."
- [Stems](/export/stems/) skip the master's limiter, so a stem can peak higher than the mix.
- When the export finishes, the sheet reports what the sound measured. See [Export progress and the report](/export/progress-and-report/).

## Related

- [Export bit depth](/export/bit-depth/)
- [Audio stems](/export/stems/)
- [Export loudness](/export/loudness/)
- [Choose a format](/export/formats/)

The **Size** popup sets the width and height of the exported file, whatever the size of your canvas. The readout under the controls always shows the numbers the file will have.

<AtAGlance
  menu="File ▸ Export…"
  keys="⌘E"
  where="Export sheet ▸ Size"
  tools="export"
/>

## Choose a size

Open the export sheet and pick a row in **Size**. Each row prints its numbers, for example `1080p · 1920 × 1080`.

| Row | What it writes |
| --- | --- |
| **GIF default** or **APNG default** | The format's cap, 480 × 270 or 960 × 540. Only on those two formats, where it's the default. |
| **Document size** | The canvas as it is. The default for every movie format. |
| **Document (even)** | Takes the place of **Document size** when the format needs [even dimensions](#odd-widths-and-heights) and the canvas has an odd edge. It's one pixel smaller on that edge. |
| **4K** | A short edge of 2160 pixels. |
| **1440p** | A short edge of 1440 pixels. |
| **1080p** | A short edge of 1080 pixels. |
| **720p** | A short edge of 720 pixels. |
| **Custom…** | The [width and height you type](#type-a-custom-size). |

The number in a row's name is the short edge. The long edge follows your canvas's shape, rounded to the nearest even number:

| Canvas | **1080p** | **4K** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1920 × 1080 | 1920 × 1080 | 3840 × 2160 |
| 1080 × 1920 (vertical) | 1080 × 1920 | 2160 × 3840 |
| 1080 × 1080 (square) | 1080 × 1080 | 2160 × 2160 |
| 3024 × 1964 | 1662 × 1080 | 3326 × 2160 |

Changing **Format** rebuilds the list and puts it back on that format's first row, so a size picked for a movie doesn't follow you into a GIF.

## Type a custom size

<Steps>

1. Choose **Custom…** in **Size**. The two fields on the row below come live, holding the size that was chosen a moment before.

2. Type a width and a height, from 16 to 8192 pixels each.

3. Press <kbd>Return</kbd> or <kbd>Tab</kbd>, or click elsewhere. The readout updates then, not on each keystroke. Choosing **Export…** does the same.

</Steps>

A number outside the range stays in the field, and **Export…** beeps until you fix it. With a field empty, **Export…** and **Add to Queue** are greyed out and the readout says "Type a width and a height, or pick a size from the list."

## Sizes that repeat

A row with the same numbers as an earlier row is hidden, so one size shows once, under the name that says more. A 1920 × 1080 document shows **Document size** and no separate **1080p**.

A saved preset that names a hidden row still works. It lands on the row showing the same numbers.

## Export larger than the document

The list offers sizes larger than the document, so a 720p recording can go out at 4K for a platform that picks its bit rate by resolution.

A movie is scaled up to the size you choose. The picture is drawn at the canvas size first, so a larger frame holds more pixels but no more detail.

GIF and APNG are never enlarged. See [Good to know](#good-to-know).

## Odd widths and heights

H.264, HEVC, HEVC with Alpha, HEVC 10-bit, both AV1 formats, both VP9 formats and ProRes 422 need even dimensions. On these formats an odd width or height is written one pixel smaller, and the readout shows the size the file will really have. This applies to a custom size as well as to the canvas.

ProRes 4444, GIF and APNG keep an odd edge.

## A different shape from the canvas

A movie is written at exactly the size you choose. What happens to the picture depends on how close that size is to the canvas's shape:

- **Within a pixel of the canvas's shape**, the picture fills the frame edge to edge, with no black line along an edge.
- **Any other shape** is letterboxed with black.

Only **Custom…** can give you a different shape, because every row in the list has the canvas's shape.

ProRes 4444, HEVC with Alpha and VP9 with Alpha (WebM) don't letterbox, because the padding would destroy the alpha channel. An odd size typed in those proportions is fine. See [Transparent exports](/export/transparency/).

## Good to know

- GIF and APNG fit the picture inside the size you choose, keeping its shape and never enlarging it, so they have no letterbox. Their rows show the fitted numbers: a 1080 × 1920 project's **GIF default** is 152 × 270. See [Animated GIF and PNG](/export/gif-and-apng/).
- **Size** is greyed out for the [audio-only formats](/export/audio-only/).
- A preset stores the row you chose rather than its numbers, so "4K" comes out at the right 4K size for each document. See [Export presets](/export/presets/).

## Related

- [Canvas size](/projects/canvas-size/)
- [Export quality](/export/quality/)
- [Export frame rate](/export/frame-rate/)

---
title: Export frame rate
description: Export at the project's own frame rate, or at a fixed rate from 23.976 to 60 fps.
---

import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';

The **Frame rate** popup sets how many frames a second the exported file has, without changing the project.

<AtAGlance
  menu="File ▸ Export…"
  keys="⌘E"
  where="Export sheet ▸ Frame rate"
  tools="export"
/>

## Choose a frame rate

Open the export sheet and pick a row in **Frame rate**. The readout under the controls shows the rate the file will have.

| Row | What it writes |
| --- | --- |
| **Project rate** | The default. The document's [frame rate](/projects/frame-rate/), or the format's own rate for Animated GIF (12.5 fps) and Animated PNG (25 fps). |
| **24 fps**, **23.976 fps** | Film rates. |
| **25 fps** | |
| **30 fps**, **29.97 fps** | |
| **50 fps** | |
| **60 fps** | |

Frame Job draws the same timeline at the instants of the rate you pick, so the length stays the same and only the number of frames changes.

## What else the rate changes

- **The range.** The start and length of the export are snapped to the export's frame grid, which moves each by less than a frame. See [Export a range](/export/range/).
- **The bit rate.** A faster rate takes a higher video rate. The [Quality](/export/quality/) tiers rise by half above 30.5 fps, and each tier's title shows the new number.
- **The time an AV1 or VP9 export takes.** The estimate in the readout counts frames, so it follows the rate.

## Good to know

- **Frame rate** is greyed out for the [audio-only formats](/export/audio-only/), which have no frames.
- A fixed rate is remembered with the rest of the sheet, and every document's sheet opens on it. Check it before you export a project with a different rate. Choose **Project rate** to go back. See [The export sheet](/export/export-sheet/).
- A preset stores the rate you chose. **Project rate** stays **Project rate**, so it follows each document.

## With an agent

An agent can't set the frame rate. Its `export` uses the document's rate, or the format's own rate for GIF and APNG. See [Export: start, then poll](/mcp/export/).

## Related

- [Project frame rate](/projects/frame-rate/)
- [Export size](/export/size/)
- [Export quality](/export/quality/)

---
title: Encoder speed
description: Choose how long the AV1 encoder works on each frame, trading export time against file size.
---

import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';

AV1 is encoded in software, so it takes longer than the HEVC formats, which use your Mac's hardware encoder. The **Speed** row sets how long the encoder works on each frame: longer gives a smaller file.

<AtAGlance
  menu="File ▸ Export…"
  keys="⌘E"
  where="Export sheet ▸ Speed"
  tools="export"
/>

## Choose a speed

In the export sheet, choose **AV1 (MP4)** or **AV1 (WebM)** in **Format**, then pick a row in **Speed**. The row sits under **Format**, or under **Dynamic Range** in an HDR project.

| Speed | What it does | SVT-AV1 preset |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Faster** | The quickest export and the largest file. | 8 |
| **Balanced** | The default. | 6 |
| **Smaller file** | The slowest export and the smallest file. | 4 |

The footnote names your choice, for example `AV1 · MP4 · Balanced`, and the estimate in the readout follows it, for example `Estimated time: about 25 s`. The estimate is only a guide. Its figures come from an idle Apple M2 Max, so a slower or busy Mac, or a heavy timeline, takes longer.

The rate from [Quality](/export/quality/) is the cap at every speed, and each speed is tuned to match HEVC's picture at that rate. So Speed moves the time and the file size, not the quality you asked for.

## What each speed costs

Measured on 10 seconds of 4K camera footage on an Apple M2 Max, exported as AV1 (MP4):

| Speed | Time at 4K | File at 4K | Time at 1080p | File at 1080p |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Faster** | 7.1 s | 27 % larger than Balanced | 2.4 s | 4 % larger than Balanced |
| **Balanced** | 14.0 s | | 4.2 s | |
| **Smaller file** | 19.9 s | 12 % smaller than Balanced | 5.8 s | 5 % smaller than Balanced |

Speed changes the memory an export uses too. **Faster** measured about 1.4 GB at 1080p and 4.9 GB at 4K, **Balanced** about 2.4 GB and 8.0 GB, and **Smaller file** about 2.6 GB and 8.7 GB. That decides how long a job can wait in [the Export Queue](/export/export-queue/).

## Good to know

- On every other format **Speed** is greyed out and keeps your last choice. That includes VP9 (WebM) and VP9 with Alpha (WebM), because VP9 has one speed.
- The choice is remembered with the rest of the sheet and stored in [presets](/export/presets/).

## Related

- [AV1 and VP9](/export/av1-and-vp9/)
- [Export quality](/export/quality/)
- [The Export Queue](/export/export-queue/)
